content_items.title: Governance as a Foundation for Resilient Biodiversity Data Infrastructures: Lessons from DiSSCo

programme.title: Governance as a Foundation for Resilient Biodiversity Data Infrastructures: Lessons from DiSSCo
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract:
Governance as a Foundation for Resilient Biodiversity Data Infrastructures: Lessons from DiSSCo RI

Building resilient biodiversity data infrastructures depends equally on governance systems that sustain coordination, legitimacy, adaptability, and long-term service provision. As biodiversity science increasingly relies on distributed research infrastructures connecting institutions, collections, and communities across national and international scales, governance becomes a critical enabling component of resilience.

Resilient infrastructures require support from multiple stakeholder groups, including funding authorities, service providers, and strategic partners. Effective governance provides mechanisms through which these actors contribute to strategic direction, operational implementation, and continuous evolution of infrastructure services, ensuring alignment between scientific priorities, user needs, and sustainability objectives.

Here we explore governance as a foundational pillar through the case of DiSSCo (Distributed System of Scientific Collections). DiSSCo applies a multi-level governance model distinguishing decision-making, executive, implementation, and advisory functions, connecting a central coordination structure with a distributed network of national and institutional actors. This approach strengthens transparency, accountability, and responsiveness while supporting sustained service delivery and innovation.

The DiSSCo experience distils transferable lessons, including mechanisms for cross-layer communication, integration of independent advisory functions, and alignment with shared strategic priorities. Governance is not a supporting component of research infrastructures; it is a fundamental condition for their resilience and enduring scientific impact.

actual.identification_notes: Eva Alonso introduces herself as co-chair from Naturalis and announces her governance talk; content matches the abstract. She presented without speaker notes after a slide/remote-desktop problem; questions were deferred to the session discussion.

content_items.summary: Eva Alonso argues that governance is a "connective tissue" that makes research infrastructures resilient, distinguishing operational governance (budget, legal form, decision processes) from strategic-capability governance. Using DiSSCo, which becomes operational next year, she shows how inclusiveness is built into its statutes through a Nodes Advisory Committee and strategic agreements with third parties, and how keeping funders close (Funders Forum, then an Interim Council of more than 18 countries) brought nodes into national roadmaps. She also points to a Dutch coordination of 15 health and life-science infrastructures as a way to counter funding fragmentation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Inclusive, funder-connected governance designed into a research infrastructure from day one is a core ingredient of its resilience.
content_items.why_it_matters: Most resilience talk focuses on technology; this frames governance structures, funder relations and cross-infrastructure coordination as practical levers that decide whether infrastructures like DiSSCo survive political and funding shocks.
key_points: Governance has two layers: operational mechanics (budget cycle, regulations, legal form, who decides how) and strategic-capability governance that lets infrastructures underpin competitiveness, innovation and resilience.

Three governance elements matter most: inclusiveness of key actors from day one, facilitating translation of science into societally beneficial measures, and advocating against funding fragmentation and bias.

DiSSCo's governance looks conventional (General Assembly, Director General, Executive Board, advisory bodies, national nodes), but its Nodes Advisory Committee is written into the statutes and advises on strategic direction.
The statutes allow strategic agreements with third parties that are neither members nor funders but want to contribute to the mission.
Keeping funders close took at least five years, moving from a non-decision-making Funders Forum to a decision-making Interim Council of more than 18 countries.
Funding fragmentation pushes institutions into opportunistic behaviour; coordinated advocacy by several infrastructures (e.g. 15 Dutch health and life-science RIs) can counter it.
Trade-offs remain: uncertain durability of joint governance, preserving uniqueness, tracing impact in short political cycles, and keeping people engaged.

notable_claims.claim: Through the DiSSCo Interim Council, nodes entered national roadmaps, with more than 300 million euros of investment.
Bringing funders into DiSSCo governance was a slow process taking at least five years.
Funding fragmentation deviates institutions and infrastructures from their mission by making them opportunistic.

recommendations: Design governance to be inclusive from day one, identifying key actors including policymakers and strategic partners.
Keep funders closely involved in governance to align with national priorities and secure long-term sustainability.
Coordinate with other research infrastructures to make joint value cases to governments against funding fragmentation.
Keep governance flexible and avoid administrative overhead.
results_findings: DiSSCo funder engagement led to nodes entering national roadmaps and more than 300 million euros of investment.
limitations: Hard to know how long joint governance arrangements will endure or how to preserve an institution's uniqueness within them.
Tracing benefits and impact is difficult in an evolving political context with short political cycles.
examples_case_studies: DiSSCo governance model (Nodes Advisory Committee, strategic agreements, Interim Council).
Coordination of 15 Dutch health and life-science research infrastructures lobbying for a national roadmap.

representative_excerpt.text: Second one is the funders and facilities, because keeping funders close to your heart really means that you have long-term sustainability for the research infrastructure.

notable_moments.description: Two levels of governance: operational versus strategic capability.
Governance framed as internal and external connective tissue; three key elements listed.
DiSSCo's Nodes Advisory Committee as statutory inclusiveness.
Interim Council of 18+ countries and resulting national investments.
Key messages and trade-offs of governance for resilience.

content_items.title: Resilience of Research Infrastructures through knowledge and engagement

programme.title: Resilience of Research Infrastructures through knowledge and engagement
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract:
Data and research infrastructures provide a constantly growing variety of high-quality data, yet the potential of this data often remains unexploited, sometimes to the point of challenging the capacity of the infrastructure to remain relevant beyond the lifecycle of projects or similar initiatives.

For data infrastructures to be sustainable and resilient their services must be utilized. This requires the knowledge of existing datasets and their benefits by potential users, as well as data literacy skills to search for, retrieve, and combine them in a targeted manner. By the same token, long-term usability of data infrastructures calls not only for technical and financial support but also for an active engagement effort that reaches out to create alignment with other initiatives, boosts uptake of new developments for the widest possible audience, and makes data visible and attractive over time. Hence, communication and a community of practice is crucial.

Education, training, communication, and engagement are, therefore, decisive elements to make the best of existing data infrastructures and turn them into true spaces for exchange and networking where users can discuss methods and use cases and propose new research questions.

The presentation discusses challenges and potential solutions for the sustainable use of research infrastructures and emphasizes in particular the importance of community building as well as targeted education and training initiatives.

actual.identification_notes: Co-presented: a communications officer addressed as "Jose" (surname not given in the recording) covered communication and engagement, then Mareike Petersen (programme speaker) covered training and knowledge. Mareike says she led an outreach and communication subcommittee in "TEDRIC" (ASR; probably the TETTRIs project, also rendered "Tetrik"); a colleague "Deb" is mentioned as co-author.

content_items.summary: The talk argues that resilience is not only a technical reaction to disruption but a pre-emptive strength that comes from being used, valued, understood, connected and relevant to a broad community. Jose describes a communication loop (visibility turned into understanding, use and reported impact, which builds community support) and an engagement loop (dialogue with other initiatives leading to alignment and expanded relevance). Mareike Petersen adds that infrastructures need sustained, user-centred training adapted to how users want to learn, and should treat training of end users as reinvestment in the infrastructure.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Communication, engagement and continuous user training make an infrastructure relevant enough that a community will want it to survive.
content_items.why_it_matters: It gives technically minded infrastructure teams a concrete model for how outreach and training contribute to resilience, and argues that investment in people and users should match investment in servers.
key_points: Two kinds of resilience: reactive/technical (respond to disruption) and pre-emptive, community-based resilience built on solid foundations.
A resilient infrastructure is technically robust but also used, valuable (with demonstrable value), understood, connected/interoperable and relevant to a broad community.
Communication loop: make work visible, turn visibility into understanding of why it matters, drive use, then report impact so a community supports you.
Engagement loop: communications staff can initiate dialogue with other initiatives, enabling technical alignment that expands the infrastructure into new ecosystems.
Training must be user-centred: know who users are, how they want to be trained (week-long workshop vs. scattered sessions), and which skills suit self-paced courses vs. interactive workshops.
Infrastructures need not train in everything (e.g. general research data management) that other parties already cover.
Past training mostly targeted infrastructure builders or single tool launches; continuous end-user training is needed for sustainability.

notable_claims.claim: Resilient infrastructures are those that are used, valuable, understood, connected and relevant for a sufficiently broad community, not only technically robust.
Only if a community can see what an infrastructure does, why it matters and that it works will it support it.

recommendations: Know your users and their needs and adapt training to them.
Invest sustained effort in people and end users, not just server infrastructure.
Make visible not just what you have but why it matters, and offer incentives.
Report impact.
Engage and learn from other infrastructures.
examples_case_studies: BHL's community support during its difficulties cited as an example of community-backed resilience.

representative_excerpt.text: And we are investing a lot of money, personal staff in building infrastructures, and I think we also should invest a lot into our end users to make use of them.

notable_moments.description: Reactive technical resilience contrasted with pre-emptive community-based resilience.
The double loop of communication and engagement.
Interoperability expands an infrastructure into a new ecosystem and wider relevance.
Mareike Petersen on user-centred training portfolios.
Summary recommendations.

content_items.title: Adopting Environmental Sustainability as a Strategy to Build Resilient Data Infrastructures in Biodiversity Science

programme.title: Adopting Environmental Sustainability as a Strategy to Build Resilient Data Infrastructures in Biodiversity Science
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract:
In the aftermath of the COVID pandemic and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, ESFRI (European Strategy Forum for Research Infrastructures) reported on the challenges posed to research by high energy costs and shortages of critical resources required by scientific computing and large experimental facilities. As a response to the difficult situation, ESFRI recommended research infrastructures to increase the environmental sustainability of their operations by decreasing energy use, promoting eco-friendly processes, and increasing reuse and recycling, especially for critical resources in short supply. Since the report was published, new conflicts and geopolitical tensions have further destabilised energy markets and jeopardised the supply chain of key elements for computer hardware, such as rare earth elements. ESFRI's recommendation is now more relevant than ever.

The paper considers how data infrastructures in biodiversity science can become more resilient by adopting environmental sustainability as a guiding principle. Considering the growing amount of research data in biodiversity science and the increasing use of resource-intensive technologies like generative AI as part of research, biodiversity science can greatly benefit from understanding the environmental footprint of its data infrastructures and implement strategies to lower it. This is not only a required contribution to address global environmental challenges, such as climate change, but also a risk management strategy to reduce operational and strategic risks due to scarcity and/or high costs of energy and computing hardware, and to be prepared to comply with more stringent environmental reporting obligations that are likely to involve research infrastructures over time, at least in the European Union.

speakers.name: Giuditta Parolini
speakers.affiliation: Museum für Naturkunde Berlin – Leibniz Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity Science

actual.identification_notes: Giuditta Parolini (session co-chair, introduced herself at the start of the session) presented; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Giuditta Parolini argues that environmental sustainability, rarely discussed in research data management, should be treated as a risk-management strategy rather than a nice-to-have. Drawing on the International Energy Agency (growing demand, geopolitical fragmentation, grid limits strained by AI data centres, pressure on critical materials such as rare earths and lithium, slow climate mitigation) and a 2023 ESFRI report on energy and supply challenges, she defines resilience as continued availability of core services under political, legal, financial and technological change. Frugal infrastructures that need fewer resources are better placed to face rising hardware and energy costs and growing EU environmental reporting duties, and biodiversity data are especially at risk because they are politically contentious.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Building frugal, environmentally sustainable data infrastructures is a practical risk-management strategy for resilience.
content_items.why_it_matters: It reframes green IT from a values question into a resilience argument that infrastructure managers and funders can act on as energy, hardware and compliance risks grow.
key_points: Sustainability in RDM is usually discussed in financial or social terms, rarely environmental, even though IT infrastructure use of electricity, hardware and e-waste keeps growing.
The IEA identifies growing energy demand against geopolitical fragmentation and grids not keeping pace, partly due to generative-AI data centres.
Supply chains for critical materials are under pressure (e.g. the 2025 Chinese export restrictions on rare earths; lithium provisioning).

Resilience = continued availability of core services under political, legal, financial and technological change; build it by defining core services, identifying risks and adopting a risk-management strategy.
ESFRI (2023, after COVID and the Ukraine invasion) recommended greening operations, including materials, reuse and recycling, as risk management.
Biodiversity data are politically contentious and face energy/hardware cost risks plus EU environmental regulation and reporting duties.

notable_claims.claim: Environmental sustainability of research data infrastructures is a risk-management strategy, not a nice-to-have.
The growth of the data-centre industry driven by generative AI is putting electric grids under pressure in many countries.
ESFRI's 2023 report recommended that research infrastructures green their operations, including materials, reuse and recycling.

recommendations: Build biodiversity data infrastructures with environmental sustainability in mind to make them more resilient.
Identify core services, the risks to them, and a risk-management strategy.

representative_excerpt.text: If you have a frugal infrastructure, this infrastructure is going to face less risks when hardware is going to cost 10 times more than it used to cost a few years ago

notable_moments.description: International Energy Agency risk analysis.
Definition of resilience as continued availability of core services.
ESFRI 2023 report on energy and supply challenges.
Take-home message.

content_items.title: Supporting resilient data infrastructure in a changing environment

programme.title: Supporting resilient data infrastructure in a changing environment
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract: Recent concurrent losses of funding, people, and institutional support for U.S. environmental data infrastructure has forced a reckoning with the vulnerabilities of our previous systems. U.S. environmental data infrastructures, both human and technical, are more fragile than had been widely understood, often lacking sustainable funding, robust policies, and programmatic protections. Initial triage responses by data users and professionals were fragmented and relied heavily on copying data and information to repositories perceived as stable, often housed outside the U.S. As data rescue efforts expanded, we increased coordination and collaboration, and reduced fragmentation as groups communicated to share practices and identify high-priority datasets and products. In the last several months, the focus has shifted to improving the usability of data and products, including recreating and expanding lost environmental data services on new hosts. Data professionals have also built tools for assisting repositories in assessing resilience and planning for improved sustainability. Beyond the data itself, there has been a growing recognition that preserving and sharing knowledge about data infrastructures-methodologies, processes, and people, as well as analyses and applications-is critical for making data useful in the future. We will share reflections from a range of environmental data professionals and organizations on how to design and construct new data ecosystems that are more resilient and prepared for future challenges, and that preserve expertise, institutional knowledge and access to environmental data and knowledge.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduces herself as "Rachel Blake" (ASR spelling) from Intertidal Agency, a US nonprofit; matches the programme.

content_items.summary: Rachael Blake reviews how sudden US funding and personnel changes in 2025 exposed fragile environmental data systems, with examples such as EJSCREEN, the NOAA Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database and Columbia's SEDAC being lost or rehosted. She describes how panic copying without metadata or context fragmented data, while informed rescuers rebuilt datasets on Zenodo, domain repositories or bespoke hosting (e.g. EPA Risk Management Plan data via Datasette). She then surveys efforts toward long-term resilient systems and argues for investing in human infrastructure, interoperability, federated networks and purpose-driven data products.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Technical copies are not enough: durable data infrastructure depends on preserved human expertise, messy maintenance work and data standardized close to collection.
content_items.why_it_matters: It distils lessons from the 2025 US data-rescue wave that biodiversity infrastructures can apply before a crisis hits.
key_points: In early 2025 the US community risked losing entire archives and repositories; patched fragile systems broke when funding and staff changed.

Examples: EJSCREEN (now hosted by Public Environmental Data Partners), the Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database (now at Climate Central), SEDAC (shut down; data archived at NASA and Harvard Dataverse).
Panic copying without context or metadata fragmented data and did not support long-term interoperability or reuse.
Short-term recovery used domain and generalist repositories (much went to Zenodo) and bespoke architectures; EPA RMP data served via Datasette as SQLite.
Longer-term efforts: repository crisis scorecards, Climate Reserve at the Aspen Global Change Institute supporting former federal staff, the Council of Data Facilities on replication.
Coalitions: Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure, AGU Global Data Convening, Semantic Commons for Climate, Nature and Economy, World Ocean Database resilience effort.
Training the next generation of data stewards (e.g. an ocean data stewardship programme launched this year).

content_items.title: From Pixels to Policy: Closing the Gap between In Situ Monitoring, Earth Observation, and Policy Actionability

programme.title: From Pixels to Policy: Closing the Gap between In Situ Monitoring, Earth Observation, and Policy Actionability
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract:
Scaling biodiversity monitoring requires aligning multi-level observations - from field sensors to satellite imagery - with international policy targets such as the CBD Global Biodiversity Framework and the UNDRR Sendai Framework. As thematic architectures like the EU’s Biodiversity Data Space are established, a process exemplified by the Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD) project, the focus is shifting from simple data mobilization toward robust knowledge governance. The primary challenge is ensuring long-term digital resilience and persistent legal actionability for stakeholders, from policy-makers to Natura 2000 managers.

We address this by applying FAIR Digital Objects (FDOs) as "Actionable Knowledge Units" to bridge the gap between field deployments and regulatory requirements. We employ the WildLIVE Monitoring Ontology (WLMO) to link sensor deployments with biological events. By integrating the European Legislation Identifier (ELI) and the Open Digital Rights Language (ODRL), observations are mapped to frameworks such as the EU’s Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 and the Nature Restoration Law. Converting static legal text into machine-interpretable policy objects enables automated governance over data processing and access.

This approach ensures that critical environmental data remains a stable, machine-actionable cornerstone for conservation. We demonstrate this through three implementations: the Socotra Data Portal, safeguarding socio-ecological records in Yemen; the WildLIVE platform, integrating edge sensors with Earth Observation; and the Movebank database, providing harmonization and a digital security layer for heterogeneous biodiversity data.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduced as "Klaus Wallen from Senckenberg" (ASR for Claus Weiland); co-lead from the Senckenberg science-policy unit rendered "Aydin Yumur" (spelling uncertain). Talk content (Pixel to Policy, FAIR digital objects, WLMO) matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Claus Weiland presents a "Pixel to Policy" approach for making endangered earth and environmental data rescue-ready, within the new DFG-funded SEND Earth Data project that aims at preservation workflows with legal guidance, resilient storage and a national data-sovereignty network grounded in NFDI4Earth and aligned with the AGU global data resilience framework. Use cases include camera-trap data from Polissya (Ukraine) with the Frankfurt Zoological Society, multidisciplinary monitoring from Socotra (Yemen), and redundant storage for Movebank tracking data. Data, annotations, Earth-observation links, machine-readable policies and workflow provenance are packaged as FAIR Digital Objects built on web standards (schema.org, RO-Crate, Bioschemas, Croissant) - "WebFDO" - with a Wildlife Monitoring Ontology and ODRL-based policy objects serving as "data lifeboats".
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Packaging data with its semantics, provenance and machine-readable policy as FAIR Digital Objects makes it rescue-ready and redeployable elsewhere.
content_items.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete technical pattern for moving at-risk biodiversity and environmental data between infrastructures without losing the legal and policy context that makes it usable.
key_points: Data at risk from institutional defunding, reprioritization toward security and AI, and armed conflict.

SEND Earth Data (Secure Endangered Earth Data), DFG-funded and started two months ago, delivers preservation workflows with legal guidance and usage agreements, resilient storage and a national data-sovereignty network grounded in NFDI4Earth.

Use cases: Polissya camera traps (Ukraine, with Frankfurt Zoological Society), Socotra monitoring (Yemen, with the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature, Jordan), redundant storage for Movebank.

A capture event links images, ML annotations, DNA from samples, Earth-observation time series, machine-readable policies, licences and workflow provenance; drawing a software "box" around it with an identifier and type makes a FAIR Digital Object.
WebFDO uses schema.org/JSON-LD, RO-Crate, Bioschemas and MLCommons Croissant; DiSSCo digital specimens are the same concept.
Wildlife Monitoring Ontology (WLMO), derived from SOSA, with mappings to Camtrap DP via SSSOM.
Policy embedded with ODRL permissions and duties and the European Legislation Identifier ontology (from Biodiversity Meets Data), e.g. linking to the Nature Restoration Law.
Envisioned multi-tier resiliency network from national (NFDI) through European (DiSSCo, EOSC/Data Terra) to the AGU global framework.

content_items.title: The GBIF data index: crawling and crawled

programme.title: The GBIF data index: crawling and crawled
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract: The GBIF data infrastructure indexes over 120,000 datasets from 2,700 institutions, and maintains a website and public API sharing over 3.7 billion species occurrences. GBIF runs a crawler to retrieve datasets for indexing, and is accessed by crawlers. We will share how our approach to crawling data has changed over the last 20 years, the impact AI bots and AI users have made on the system, and ongoing challenges we face in maintaining a reliable service.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduces himself as Matthew Blissett, GBIF software developer responsible for infrastructure resilience; matches programme.

content_items.summary: Matthew Blissett traces how GBIF moved from distributed DiGIR/TAPIR/BioCASe queries to a central occurrence index (2007) and now weekly Darwin Core Archive downloads and image caching, and then describes how usage patterns changed in the last two to three years. Search engines and self-identifying LLM crawlers can be rate-limited or blocked (one that ignores robots.txt was blocked), but 'vibe-coded' apps now hammer the GBIF API with millions of inefficient requests, and residential-proxy networks such as Bright Data send one or two requests per IP while posing as browsers. Cloudflare blocks less than half; GBIF has had to simplify and cache web pages, categorize traffic and push monthly cloud exports, while resisting API keys.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: AI-era crawling through residential proxies is a new, hard-to-block load that is forcing open biodiversity infrastructures and their publishers to spend effort on defence.
content_items.why_it_matters: It documents a concrete, growing operational threat to open biodiversity data services and to small publishers whose public image URLs are scraped directly.
key_points: Early 2000s DiGIR/TAPIR/BioCASe fan-out searches were unreliable; from 2007 GBIF built a central index, crawling publishers with a distributed lock of one request per server.
Now nearly all publishing uses Darwin Core Archives or data packages; GBIF checks weekly and respects HTTP Not Modified.
GBIF caches publisher images for at least a year; from early spring this year publishers were overwhelmed by probable LLM-training crawlers fetching public image URLs directly.
LLM services open thousands of simultaneous connections, unlike past crawlers.
Search engines and identifying LLM crawlers respecting robots.txt are manageable; one major crawler ignoring it was blocked outright.
Since March 2025 vibe-coded apps (e.g. "Bird.world", "BioTag") make inefficient API use; over 100 sites made more than 100,000 requests in recent months.
Residential proxy networks (e.g. Bright Data via apps on smart TVs) make crawling almost unidentifiable; Cloudflare blocks less than half.
Mitigations: simpler, daily-cached pages, request categorization, pre-calculated data, extended monthly cloud exports; GBIF does not want API keys.

notable_claims.claim: One vibe-coded app makes about six million requests per day for data that could be a single download obtained in 15 minutes.
Over 100 such sites have made over 100,000 requests to GBIF in the last few months.
Cloudflare does not block more than half of the residential-proxy crawler traffic.

results_findings: Residential-proxy crawlers send one or two requests per IP per month and pretend to be browsers, making them very hard to identify.
future_work: Continue categorizing requests, pre-calculating data and extending monthly cloud uploads.

representative_excerpt.text: So the new crawling that is really difficult to block, we get one or two requests from an IP address. That's it for the month.

notable_moments.description: History: from distributed queries to a central occurrence index.
Publishers overwhelmed by LLM crawlers fetching images.
Vibe-coded apps hammering the GBIF API.
How residential proxy networks work.
GBIF reluctance to introduce API keys.

content_items.title: Resilient Attribution Infrastructures for Biodiversity Science: Archiving and Risk Mitigation in Bionomia

programme.title: Resilient Attribution Infrastructures for Biodiversity Science: Archiving and Risk Mitigation in Bionomia
programme.session: SYM18: Building resilient data infrastructures for biodiversity science
programme.abstract:
Bionomia is an independent biodiversity data infrastructure that links natural history specimens shared through GBIF to the people who collected and identified them. The platform focuses on creating durable, attributable connections between biodiversity records and human expertise, particularly for collectors whose contributions are often obscured in downstream aggregations.

This presentation explores how Bionomia is adopting resilience-oriented practices in response to increasing infrastructural instability, including governance uncertainty, AI-driven scraping pressure, dependence on centralized services, and sustainability risks facing small biodiversity informatics projects. Rather than functioning solely as a web application, Bionomia increasingly treats itself as a distributed archival workflow. Public claims and profile datasets are versioned and deposited to Zenodo, creating DOI-backed snapshots that remain citable, reproducible, and recoverable even if operational infrastructure changes or disappears.

The talk will highlight practical strategies for resilience, including automated archival deposition, integration with ORCID and Wikidata identifiers, open-source reconciliation tools, and interoperable data products that can be mirrored or reused by other infrastructures.

Bionomia offers a case study in both the vulnerabilities and strengths of independently maintained scientific infrastructure, demonstrating how small projects can experiment with preservation, attribution, and reuse models under uncertain technological and political conditions.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video by the maintainer of Bionomia (David Shorthouse, virtual); the video started a second time at 01:29:18 and was stopped. Shorthouse also joined the discussion live via Zoom.

content_items.summary: David Shorthouse describes Bionomia, which links more than 50 million biodiversity records to people via ORCID and Wikidata identifiers through automation and volunteer 'scribes', and the risks it faces: code and server upkeep, institutional oversight questions with his employer, and AI crawlers that took the site down dozens of times until Cloudflare was introduced. Resilience comes from simple design, standalone libraries (a Ruby gem ported to Go for parsing human names), and monthly archiving to Zenodo of a CSV graph and frictionless data packages for roughly 9,000 GBIF datasets, which institutions such as the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo reuse. Small projects can be resilient if they plan for decommissioning from the outset.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Small niche infrastructures can be resilient by planning for their own end: keep things simple and push versioned data and reusable code outward.

content_items.title: An Introduction to the Biodiversity Data Quality Standard (BDQ)

programme.title: An Introduction to the Biodiversity Data Quality Standard (BDQ)
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract:
The quality of biodiversity data is a critical determinant of its utility for science and policy. TheBiodiversity Data Quality (BDQ) standard is a comprehensive, modular and flexible framework designed to assess the "fitness for use" of biodiversity data records.

The development of BDQ has been an 12-year journey. The need was realized at 2010 TDWG in Woods Hole. Work began in 2014 with the establishment of the BDQ Interest Group and its Task Groups. This work resulted in the 2020 publication "Developing Standards for Improved Data Quality" and the subsequent submission of BDQ in 2025.

The BDQ framework is anchored in the Fitness for Use Framework Ontology (bdqffdq) to provide the underlying semantics for data quality needs and solutions. Supporting this ontology are specialized vocabularies that define tests (e.g., Empty, ActedUpon), data quality dimensions (e.g., Completeness, Conformance), criteria (e.g., Found, Standard) and enhancements (e.g., Converted, Standardized).

110 core Single-record tests are the heart of BDQ. They are categorized into fourTest Types: Validation - Factchecking (e.g., VALIDATION_LATITUDE_INRANGE), returning results like COMPLIANT or NOT_COMPLIANT; Issue - Flag potential problems (e.g., ISSUE_ANNOTATION_NOTEMPTY); Amendment - Proposes improvements (e.g., AMENDMENT_MONTH_STANDARDIZED) and Measure - Metrics that quantify quality (e.g., MEASURE_AMENDMENTS_PROPOSED).

The standard explicitly supports two primary data management workflows: Quality Control (QC): Focuses on identifying and remediating errors to improve a dataset-the "run → analyze patterns → fix causes → re-run" loop. Quality Assurance (QA): Focuses on filtering records to ensure only those fit for a specific use, such as species distribution modeling, are used in analysis.

actual.identification_notes: Lee Belbin chaired the session and gave the first talk; he thanks team members Arthur, Paul and John. Matches programme.

content_items.summary: Lee Belbin introduces the proposed TDWG Biodiversity Data Quality (BDQ) standard: a unified, transparent framework of 110 core single-record tests derived from reviewing over 500 tests run by aggregators. Tests take information elements (Darwin Core as example, but data-structure agnostic), parameters and source authorities, and are of four types (validations, amendments, issues, measures) described in seven vocabularies and one ontology. He stresses that data quality cannot be defined without a use case, that tests should be applied from the point of collection onward, and mentions using Gemini Notebooks with the ~800 pages of documentation to prepare the slides.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: BDQ provides 110 standard, use-case-linked tests so that data quality can be assessed consistently from collection to aggregation.
content_items.why_it_matters: A shared data quality test suite would let publishers, aggregators and users assess fitness for use consistently instead of each running idiosyncratic checks.
key_points: Work started from the idea at Woods Hole in 2010 and was convened from 2014; it took far longer than the expected year and a half.
Over 500 tests from aggregators (ALA, GBIF, iDigBio, BISON, etc.) were reviewed to build a single framework.
Output: 110 core single-record tests and four use cases; adding a test requires justifying it by a use case (tutorial and BDQUC vocabulary).
Tests use information elements, parameters and source authorities (e.g. ISO 3166) and are independent of Darwin Core, ABCD or data packages.
Four test types: validation (e.g. country found), amendment (e.g. month standardized, not to be applied without consideration), issue (e.g. annotation not empty, some tests aspirational) and measure.
Seven vocabularies and one ontology (BDQ FFDQ) underpin the standard.
Cradle-to-grave approach: ideally apply tests at collection (e.g. in Specify or field apps) as well as by aggregators.

notable_claims.claim: BDQ comprises 110 core single-record tests.
Over 500 tests run by data aggregators were reviewed when developing the framework.
Data quality cannot be defined without a use case.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Task Group 3 of the Data Quality Interest Group surveyed potential use cases; the team took some, added one and removed others, ending with four use cases; a tutorial explains how to add new use cases and tests.

representative_excerpt.text: and I think one of the key take home messages is you cannot define data quality without a use case.

content_items.title: GBIF Rule Based Annotations

programme.title: GBIF Rule Based Annotations
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract:
Biodiversity data quality is commonly run through automated tests and standardized assertions, yet many data quality issues are not captured by existing pipelines.

We present rule-based annotations as a practical approach for translating informal expert knowledge into structured, reusable data quality rules. Simple statements such as “there are no dragonflies in Antarctica” can be formalized as rules linking taxa, geography, and controlled vocabularies (e.g. suspicious, native, introduced), and applied to both current and future occurrence records.

Unlike traditional cleaning approaches or one-off feedback to data publishers, rule-based annotations are persistent, shareable, and extensible. Rules can incorporate additional constraints (e.g. basis of record, time, dataset) and are managed through an experimental community-driven system. This enables a flexible, opinion-based layer of data quality assessment that complements existing standards and automated checks .

We demonstrate the approach using a case study on Odonata, where expert-defined rules identify a small number of outliers not captured by standard cleaning pipelines, yet with disproportionate effects on downstream species distribution models.

Just as filtering rules in an email inbox serve to filter and sort incoming emails, rule based annotations are meant to be future looking. Once a rule is created it is saved to a database, and is accessible to all GBIF users. Users can leave comments and upvote or downvote based on their perception of the general usefulness of the rule.

actual.identification_notes: John Waller introduces himself from GBIF; the wrong slide file was loaded so he switched to his laptop while talking. A few seconds of Cristian-Dan Bara's video played accidentally at 02:51:39 (excluded).

content_items.summary: John Waller presents experimental work at GBIF on rule-based annotations that capture 'rules in people's heads' about suspicious occurrences, e.g. 'amphibians in Antarctica are suspicious'. Rules are polygons plus taxon and optional scoping (dataset key, basis of record, fossils excluded) and apply to existing and future records. Examples include an elephant shrew record in Madagascar and axolotls outside Mexico; he argues that marking where a species is certainly not found (an 'anti-distribution') is much easier for non-experts than defining native ranges. A demo Download Annotator and an R package, gbifrules, apply rules to downloads.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Simple, scoped negative-range rules let non-experts flag suspicious GBIF occurrences persistently, including future records.
content_items.why_it_matters: It offers a lightweight, community-driven way to capture expert knowledge about data errors that survives unstable occurrence identifiers.
key_points: Rules flag all current and future matching records (taxon within polygon) as suspicious.
Anti-distributions (where a species will not occur) are easier to define than native ranges and need little expertise.
Because GBIF occurrence IDs are not fully stable, single records are targeted by scoping rules to a small box plus dataset key and basis of record.
Complex rules allow exceptions, e.g. no non-human primates in Cuba except fossils.
Tools: an experimental web UI for making rules, a browser-based Download Annotator demo, and the gbifrules R package (GitHub, not CRAN).
Main challenge: recruiting rule makers; the feature is not yet visible on gbif.org.
methods: Rule scoping by dataset key and basis of record

content_items.title: Interpreting the Responses from BDQ Tests

programme.title: Interpreting the Responses from BDQ Tests
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract:
BDQ (Biodiversity Data Quality) is a standard designed to facilitate the consistent development and use of a set of biodiversity data quality tests and responses from these tests.

The Standard takes Darwin Core (Wieczorek et al., 2011) encoded data, evaluates quality using data quality Tests and produces a report. The reporting from of BDQ Tests is the focus of this presentation (see User’s Guide to the Standard).

Tests for data quality may serve two purposes: Quality Control and Quality Assurance.

In Quality Assurance (QA), data are evaluated for fitness for use and are filtered down to those data that are fit for that use. In Quality Control (QC), tests are used to identify data that are not fit for a specific use. The goal is to improve data quality by proposing changes to the data.

A Data Quality Report, produced from running a BDQ Tests is expected to include a Response for each Test run.

In brief, each Response consists of the following elements:

Response.status - Metadata describing the status of the Test run, including whether the Test was executed successfully. Values include RUN_HAS_RESULT, INTERNAL_PREREQUISITES_NOT_MET and EXTERNAL_PREREQUISITES_NOT_MET. Response.result - The result of the evaluation of the Test against the input data. Values include "COMPLIANT", "NOT_COMPLIANT", "COMPLETE", "NOT_COMPLETE", or data values depending on the type of Test. Response.comment - A human-readable comment providing additional context or information to assist users in the interpretation of the Test result.

These responses are dependant of the type of Test - Validation, Amendment, Issue or Measure.

The presentation will discuss these issues, and various pitfalls, especially with Amendment Tests, in using the data to improve databases of record.

actual.identification_notes: Arthur Chapman introduces himself as a member of the BDQ team; matches programme.

content_items.summary: Arthur Chapman explains how to interpret the reports and responses produced by BDQ tests. The only normative output is the response, consisting of a status (e.g. run has result, internal or external prerequisites not met, amended, not amended), a result (compliant/not compliant, potential issue, a value) and a human-readable comment, plus an optional qualifier. Worked examples cover day-in-range validation, data-generalizations issue flags, day amendments and measures, with emphasis that amendments should never enter a database of record without human checking.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Every BDQ test returns a status, result and comment, and understanding these lets users decide fitness for their own use.
content_items.why_it_matters: Implementers and data users need to read BDQ outputs correctly, e.g. distinguishing data problems from temporary external failures.
key_points: Report form is not specified by BDQ, but a report should include a response for every test run, in a strict order.
Response = status (operational metadata), result (core assertion from controlled vocabulary), comment (human-readable), optional qualifier.
Internal prerequisites not met: the data cannot be evaluated and will always give this result until the record changes.
External prerequisites not met: an external authority (e.g. a GBIF vocabulary) was unavailable; rerunning may succeed.
Validation example: day 30 with month 2 of 1952 is not compliant; day 31 without a month cannot be evaluated.
Issue tests (e.g. data generalizations not empty) raise warnings for human judgement.
Measures: single-record direct, single-record derived and multi-record.

notable_claims.claim: The response is the only normative output structure of BDQ tests; how reports are presented is not defined by the standard.
Proposed amendments should not be put into a database of record until checked by a human.

recommendations: Do not apply amendments to your database of record without human checking.
Rerun tests that fail due to unmet external prerequisites.

q_and_a.answer_summary: The chairs said they had hoped the developer would present and invited them to the afternoon BDQ workshop.

representative_excerpt.text: Tests define the information elements as input and return a response.

notable_moments.description: Status, result and comment of a response.
Internal versus external prerequisites not met.
Worked day-in-range validation examples.

programme.title: The Swedish experience on verification and how to improve quality on observations
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract: Quality on observations is always a challenge as we often know was needed but human and/or economic resources are lacking. Today technical validation is well implemented in most observations system (date is existing and relevant, coordinates is in a relevant area and more). AI has the last years been of great help to find anomalies in the reported observations, but it still a need for a human eye and brain to perform the last step. To get the final approved och not approved. For some observations (e.g. red listed species under debate by forestry or species under legal act as species listed in European regulation on invasive species) the verification by human is needed for companies and agencies to guarantee that the observation is correctly identified and reported from right place. Since more than 2000 years Sweden has been evolving a quality assessment of observations, both by technical validation and human verification to reach as good quality as possible. The last five years have the verification system been improved to meet new legal requirements with more strict rules and, new tools and improved education of both the users and the persons doing verification. The Swedish system will can also be used as test for the BDQ-Standard. The presentation will cover the system with verification system, categories,contract and education of people doing the verification and contract. It will also cover the results from the work with the “new” verification system in Sweden.

content_items.title: Transitivity Failures in Taxonomic Name Resolution: Implications for Botanical Dataset Construction

programme.title: Transitivity Failures in Taxonomic Name Resolution: Implications for Botanical Dataset Construction
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract: A key decision when creating datasets about plants is whether to store the scientific names as originally recorded in a data source or to resolve them to currently accepted names. When a scientific name is resolved to an accepted name, and the original name is discarded, information is lost regarding the description and taxonomic classification used in the original identification. In practice, this may have limited impact if the original and accepted names consistently resolve to the same name in future taxonomic databases. However, this depends on the transitivity of name resolution across taxonomic database versions i.e. given names X, Y, Z and taxonomic database versions v1, v2 such that X resolves to Y in v1 and Y resolves to Z in v2, is it the case that X resolves to Z in v2? If this property does not hold in general then creating datasets by storing only resolved, accepted names may create unexpected outcomes with wide-ranging consequences for botany, and biological sciences more broadly, especially in an era where large scale data analyses are becoming increasingly prevalent in addressing many real-world challenges. Using the World Checklist of Vascular Plants and World Flora Online, we demonstrate that this transitivity fails for approximately 1% and 6% of plant names, respectively, and that the number of these discrepancies increases as new taxonomy versions are released. These results highlight the importance of storing verbatim names as found and resolving them to accepted names as close to the point of end-use as possible, using the most recent taxonomic database.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduces himself as Adam Richard-Bollans, research fellow at Kew; matches programme.

content_items.summary: Adam Richard-Bollans shows that resolving names to accepted names across taxonomy versions is not transitive: a name x resolved to y in one version may not resolve to where y resolves in a later version, e.g. because heterotypic synonyms are split. Comparing World Checklist of Vascular Plants versions (2022 vs 2025), about 13,000 of ~1.4 million names (≈1%) disagree, about half at species level, implying ~0.5% species-level error in datasets that kept only accepted names, rising to 0.7% by June 2026. Errors cluster in western and southern Europe (France, Italy, Spain).
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Always keep original verbatim names so datasets can be re-resolved against the latest taxonomy.
content_items.why_it_matters: Many secondary datasets discard original names after resolution; this quantifies the silent error that introduces and shows it grows over time.
key_points: Most aggregated botanical datasets resolve names to accepted names and often discard verbatim names.
Transitivity: x→y in v1 and y→z in v2 should imply x→z in v2; heterotypic synonym splits break this.
Example: Panicum nitidum resolved to Dichanthelium dichotomum in WCVP v10 (2022), but to Dichanthelium nitidum in v14 (2025).
~13,000 of ~1.4 million names disagree (≈1%); about half at species level, some at genus level.

Error grows with time since the original version (0.5% in 2025 to 0.7% by June 2026 for a 2022 dataset).
World Flora Online results are more severe; resolving to a different taxonomy likely increases error further.

content_items.title: How Darwin Core enables harmonizing Biodiversity Data via the OSCA Consortium

programme.title: How Darwin Core enables harmonizing Biodiversity Data via the OSCA Consortium
programme.session: SYM11: Data Quality: From Standard to Practice
programme.abstract:
Digitizing vast biological and geological collections presents a significant multi-disciplinary challenge, requiring the integration of domain expertise, information technology, and robust scientific infrastructure. The Open Scientific Collections Austria (OSCA) consortium (15 museums, universities, and scientific institutions) was created to digitize Austria’s biodiversity and geological history. These collections serve as critical longitudinal baselines for researching global crises, including climate change and biodiversity loss.

Central to this initiative was the adoption of the Darwin Core (DwC)data standard, which provided the foundational framework for cross-institutional interoperability.

We developed a centralized, cloud-based Cache database designed to aggregate DwC-compliant datasets from all consortium members. This infrastructure supports a coherent workflow that facilitates high-quality data production by both technical and non-technical researchers. To ensure global reach, the system automates the publication of records to international repositories, specifically GBIF and DiSSCo.

A dedicated public Portal was developed to enhance collaboration and provide open access to Austrian scientific data. The portal allows users to search, compare, and download records in DwC format. By enabling the cross-referencing of published data, the platform assists the scientific community in quantifying available information and identifying strategic gaps for future digitization. content_items.title: AURORA - A Shiny app designed to create Darwin Core Archives from messy biodiversity datasets

programme.title: AURORA - A Shiny app designed to create Darwin Core Archives from messy biodiversity datasets
programme.session: CO3: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
programme.abstract: Biodiversity monitoring data are commonly stored in heterogeneous tabular formats, hindering standardisation, validation, and publication through public repositories. Researchers often face technical challenges, such as taxonomic variations and multiple date and geospatial format inconsistencies, that must be addressed before datasets can be submitted to global repositories like GBIF. To address these challenges, we developed the AURORA Shiny application that provides an intuitive, end-to-end workflow for transforming raw datasets into publication-ready Darwin Core tables. The application supports data ingestion from diverse tabular formats, enabling users to convert raw datasets into tidy data format. An interactive mapping interface allows users to align user-specific fields with Darwin Core terms by combining manual selection with automated suggestions and mandatory-field validation. The tool automates essential data-cleaning tasks for taxonomic integrity by integrating API calls to the WoRMS and GBIF Backbone Taxonomies and facilitates the use of controlled vocabulary in the Extended Measurement or Fact table. Finally, a quality control module offers diagnostics on data completeness and identifies missing key fields, providing detailed information about issues and errors for tracing and resolution. Currently, the Occurrence, Event, and extended Measurement or Fact extension DwC tables are available for export. A metadata form that follows the GBIF IPT format is provided to allow prefilling and downloading, facilitating metadata review among dataset authors. The output comprises standards-compliant DwC tables ready for publication. By streamlining these time-consuming processes into a user-friendly interface, this application reduces the technical barriers to biodiversity data mobilization and global sharing. The application is accessible to the public via a web browser by accessing https://bio-shiny.ua.pt/aurora/

programme.abstract: The Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN) is an international consortium of biodiversity biobanks and collections focussing on standards and best practices, providing access to information on > 7.1 million samples. GGBN assigns persistent identifiers (PIDs) to all object types (DNA, tissue, specimen, culture, environmental sample) and establishes relationships among these, enabling cross-linking with other infrastructures (e.g., ENA). Use of DwC-DP will further improve this. programme.title: Bridging eLTER Data Reporting Format: enabling interoperable biodiversity and ecological data publication across research infrastructures
programme.session: CO3: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
Environmental and biodiversity research infrastructures increasingly face the challenge of mobilising heterogeneous observational data across domain-specific systems, harmonizing it into FAIR data products or digital twins, while preserving semantic richness and machine-actionable interoperability. Within the eLTER Research Infrastructure, ecological and environmental measurements are distributed through the Data Reporting Format (DRF), a structured, multi-table specification designed to support multi-domain standard observational workflows through different entities.

To strengthen semantic interoperability within the broader informatics landscape, a controlled vocabulary has been developed that provides labels and definitions for DRF data specification terms and aligns them with the Darwin Core standard where conceptual equivalence exists. This mapping preserves the native expressiveness of eLTER observational structures while enabling alignment with established biodiversity data exchange mechanisms and improving discoverability across infrastructures and other TDWG-compliant systems.

Building on this, an R-based workflow has been implemented that transforms DRF datasets into Data Packages. This packaging layer facilitates FAIR and machine-actionable (“robot-ready”) data publication, while enabling downstream integration into biodiversity data infrastructures without requiring convergence toward a single monolithic data model.

This work demonstrates how infrastructure-specific reporting standards can remain fit-for-purpose while participating in a coordinated biodiversity data ecosystem through explicit semantic alignment and reusable transformation workflows. The approach provides a practical contribution to strengthening interoperability.

content_items.title: The Triple A Principle: actionability, applicability and auditability for actionable biodiversity knowledge

programme.title: A³ctionable Understanding: Action units for post-FAIR biodiversity knowledge infrastructures
programme.session: CO3: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
The FAIR Principles have made biodiversity data findable, accessible, and interoperable, but not operationally usable. A critical layer is missing between semantic representation and context-sensitive action, one that distinguishes the structural capacity of a knowledge representation to support operations (actionability) from the epistemic reliability of using it in a specific context (applicability). Conflating these has contributed to well-documented failures in conservation practice.

We introduce Action Units as formal knowledge objects that extend plan specifications within the Semantic Units Framework by making applicability conditions explicit as first-class typed components. Three types correspond to three operation classes: epistemic action units ask ‘What is the case here, and does this knowledge apply?’; transformational action units ask ‘How can available representations be processed into usable form?’; and intervention action units ask ‘What can be done in this situation to achieve a desired outcome?’ Conditional action units, i.e., executable IF-THEN rules linking SPARQL context queries to workflow triggers, enable knowledge graphs to serve as AI-ready decision-support systems.

Applied to biodiversity science, the framework addresses conservation failures and enables practitioners to identify where actionable knowledge is missing. We propose the TripleA Principle-Actionability, Applicability, and Auditability (tracing evidence and failure contexts) -as a post-FAIR guiding framework, and argue that A³ctionable Understanding-Actionability, Applicability, and Action Units-provides the representational foundation next-generation biodiversity knowledge infrastructures require.

This is a conceptual proposal; implementation is deferred to subsequent work.

He proposes three nested criteria - actionability (procedural knowledge of what to do), applicability (explicit context conditions under which it works) and auditability (evidence of where it succeeded or failed, feeding back into conditions) - and a representation using the Semantic Units Framework: action units, applicable action units and audited applicable action units, plus conditional action units with question and directive units that turn a knowledge graph into a context-sensitive decision support system. content_items.title: SFBorg: a frictionless biodiversity data exchange

programme.title: SFBorg: a frictionless biodiversity data exchange
programme.session: CO3: Semantic Interoperability and Standards Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
Background: Sharing biodiversity datasets across projects and organisations depends on common exchange formats e.g., Darwin Core Archive (DwCA), Darwin Core Data Package, or the Catalogue of Life Data Package (ColDP). These formats bundle multiple CSV, JSON, or XML files into a single compressed archive. While widely adopted, this approach has a fundamental limitation: the data is effectively inert until a recipient imports it into a database. Generation of a dataset's archive is error-prone, and introduced inconsistencies might create significant problems on the receiving end. Also, there is no standard mechanism to detect what has changed between two successive releases of the same dataset.

New information: We introduce SFBorg, a SQLite-based ecosystem for biodiversity datasets exchange centred on the Species File Group Archive (SFGA) schema. An SFGA single file is a self-contained SQLite database, allowing recipients to query and modify data immediately using standard SQL tools - no import step required. The ecosystem includes: sf, a universal converter between DwCA, ColDP, and other formats, which also computes data diffs between two SFGA archives to identify added, modified, or removed taxa, names, and synonyms; harvester, for ingesting non-standard or legacy sources; and gndb, which loads SFGA archives directly into the GNverifier PostgreSQL database. Shared functionality is centralised in the sflib library, reducing duplication and lowering the cost of adding new tools. SFBorg is currently in production use across Species File Group projects. All code is open source and available on GitHub under the MIT licence.

SQLite is a single, fast, compressible file format with a stable format supported until 2050 and accepted by the Library of Congress for archiving. The ecosystem includes a shared library, the SF conversion tool (e.g. CSV, Darwin Core, ColDP via SFGA), a Harvester for idiosyncratic datasets, GNdb for building name-resolution databases, and Hive, a taxonomic viewer/editor/validator.

content_items.title: Capitalizing the Invisible Ledger: A Cost-of-Production and Shadow Pricing Methodology for Valuing Open-Source Biodiversity Assets in India

programme.title: Capitalizing the Invisible Ledger: A Cost-of-Production and Shadow Pricing Methodology for Valuing Open-Source Biodiversity Assets in India
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract:
Open-access biodiversity repositories are fundamental for Ecosystem Condition Accounts under the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting. However, because data from decentralized networks like iNaturalist and eBird relies on civic volunteerism, it carries a nominal market price of zero and is omitted from GDP. This leads to a public-good market failure, causing suboptimal resource allocation, spatial data gaps, taxonomic biases, and unverified backlogs.

This paper introduces a reproducible valuation methodology to calculate the capitalization of crowdsourced natural data infrastructure. Analyzing India’s footprint of over 4.8 million iNaturalist observations against 62 million global occurrences on the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, we model a bottom-up framework to quantify true data production costs.

The methodology deconstructs the unit value of an observation into three non-overlapping cost layers: an infrastructure data-intake base from platform operational footprints (~₹11/observation), a field curation labor asset utilizing a shadow-wage proxy for specialized field survey hours (~₹39/observation), and a taxonomic expertise premium derived from technical consultancy rates (~₹50/observation).

Aggregating these baselines establishes a theoretical production cost of ₹100 per research-grade observation, capitalizing India’s citizen science ledger at a proxy value of ₹48.02 crore. For context, the Government of India’s official annual data collection budget across the Forest, Botanical, and Zoological Surveys stands at ₹392.58 crore. This methodology provides the baseline required to internalize data-production externalities, clear verification bottlenecks, and scale open-source biodiversity monitoring.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video introduced by moderator Melissa Liu; the speaker introduces himself as Ashwin with co-authors (ASR "Lavanya Patil and Adarsh Pradhan"). The video restarted briefly at 07:37:32 and was stopped.

content_items.summary: Ashwin A estimates the hidden production cost of India's roughly 2.8 million open-access citizen-science biodiversity observations, whose market price is zero. Building a cost model from field effort, taxonomic expertise, platform and data infrastructure and participant capital, he estimates about ₹137-676 per reusable occurrence record, compared with ₹700-3,500 for professional producers and ₹2,500-7,000 per institutional specimen output (not equivalent products). He argues open access removes the price of access, not the cost of production, and calls for recognising citizen science as productive data infrastructure and co-investing in validation and coverage.

content_items.title: From citizen observations to long-term ecological knowledge: integrating iNaturalist records into LTER framework through automated enrichment

programme.title: From citizen observations to long-term ecological knowledge: integrating iNaturalist records into LTER framework through automated enrichment
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract: Citizen science observations have become major contributors to biodiversity knowledge, generating large volumes of high-quality data through widespread volunteer participation. Much of this information is shared via global open-access platforms such as iNaturalist; however, these observations often remain outside formal long-term ecological research workflows. To address this gap, an automated R-based workflow has been developed to harvest “research-grade” iNaturalist observations occurring within sites of the Long-Term Ecosystem Research (LTER) network in Europe and transform them into enriched, research-ready data for long-term ecological analysis. The workflow identifies observations geographically located within LTER sites and classified as high quality on iNaturalist, and enriches them via automated semantic augmentation using authoritative external sources. Each record is complemented with: (i) IUCN Red List conservation status, based on geographic relevance; (ii) nativeness information (Darwin Core “establishmentMeans”), filtered by country and sourced from iNaturalist; (iii) taxon protection status under the EU Habitats and Birds Directives, retrieved from the EUNIS database; and (iv) contribution to eLTER Standard Observations. The resulting R package, “ReLTER.inatEnrich”, provides an innovative integration layer enabling citizen-generated biodiversity data to directly support structured long-term ecological research. This approach offers a dual benefit: it supplies LTER sites with a replicable and user-friendly protocol to complement existing monitoring and enables cross-site comparisons, while enhancing the scientific value of citizen science data through contextual enrichment and integration into standardized ecological frameworks.

Outputs are research-ready interactive maps, charts and tables. The benefit is dual: eLTER sites gain additional observations and spatial coverage, while volunteers can engage in co-designed campaigns and see their observations gain scientific value.

content_items.title: An eDNA Platform for Community-Powered LA River Restoration

programme.title: An eDNA Platform for Community-Powered LA River Restoration
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract: The Los Angeles River runs roughly 51 miles, confined for nearly its entire length within a concrete flood-control channel. Channelization severed the river from its floodplain, collapsing riparian and wetland habitats and biodiversity. Community organizations including Friends of the LA River and Metabolic Studio have worked to restore the river through cleanup, education, and rewilding segments. Revitalization at this scale requires a way to prioritize effort and measure success, in particular whether biodiversity is returning, and which sites will benefit. Environmental DNA (eDNA), the genetic material organisms shed into air, water, and soil, provides a snapshot of biodiversity across the tree of life from citizen scientist-collected samples, avoiding the time, labor, and specialized expertise that conventional field surveys demand. In collaboration with University of California’s CALeDNA program and community partners supported by Metabolic Studio, we implemented eDNA sampling along the LA River. To make the multi-marker, high-dimensional dataset usable, we built the eDNA Explorer platform. This platform identifies organisms from raw eDNA sequencing data, integrates ~400 remote-sensing geospatial features from Google Earth Engine, and presents results through an intuitive interface that community groups can interpret without bioinformatics expertise. GBIF occurrence data is integrated, allowing users to filter and visualize detections by geographic plausibility. Machine learning models identified environmental and site-level factors most associated with biodiversity outcomes, turning a complex dataset into actionable insights. These tools give community groups a shared evidence base to interpret restoration progress and prioritize future revitalization effort.

content_items.summary: Ryan Martin describes how community groups, land managers and Indigenous groups monitoring removal of concrete from the heavily channelized Los Angeles River used eDNA metabarcoding (12 sites, seven months, six markers) and the eDNA Explorer platform. The platform handles sequencing processing, taxonomic assignment, GBIF comparisons, seasonal analyses and random-forest community models using about 400 Google Earth Engine variables, showing concrete as a strong predictor of community composition. The work, funded by Metabolic Studio with CALeDNA at UC Santa Cruz, founded eDNA Explorer and now supports ongoing restoration monitoring.

content_items.title: Ground-Truth from the Ground Up: Community-Led Occurrence Data for Prosopis juliflora Restoration in Kutch's Climate-Stressed Drylands

programme.title: Ground-Truth from the Ground Up: Community-Led Occurrence Data for Prosopis juliflora Restoration in Kutch's Climate-Stressed Drylands
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract:
In landscapes where ecological knowledge lives in people rather than databases, citizen science cannot mean app-based observation submission alone. Kutch, Gujarat, is one such landscape, an arid dryland system where communities hold decades of firsthand knowledge about how Prosopis juliflora has moved across grasslands, salt flats, and grazing corridors. This talk presents how Climitra puts that knowledge to work as primary biodiversity data.

Community field teams operate alongside satellite-based land cover classification, not beneath it. They confirm, correct, and spatially extend the occurrence layer into zones that spectral indices routinely misclassify. Structured to Darwin Core standards and contributed to GBIF, their observations move from informal ground knowledge to citable, interoperable records usable by researchers, conservation practitioners, and automated monitoring pipelines alike.

The urgency is real. With Super El Niño conditions forecast for 2026-27, juliflora is positioned to expand precisely where drought stress weakens native grassland resistance. Community-generated occurrence data is not a supplement to remote sensing here, it is a frontline climate adaptation tool. Downstream restoration outcomes, biochar soil amendment, fuel briquette provision, and native species recovery are spatially targeted only because communities made the data research-ready.

We share protocols for structured field data collection without app dependency, quality assurance workflows, and practical pathways for making vernacular ecological knowledge interoperable with global biodiversity infrastructure.

content_items.summary: Pranav Jha describes Climitra's geospatial mapping of the invasive Prosopis juliflora in Kutch, Gujarat, which was planted from 1961 to hold back the desert and has spread to about 1.1 million hectares, depleting groundwater and raising soil salinity. Communities living with the invasion act as primary data producers through local-language voice agents and simple forms, confirming and correcting satellite classifier maps from geo foundation models in a loop that removes false positives. Locals are paid through restoration livelihoods, supported by a government mandate to remove the species.

content_items.title: The Asian Nature Challenge as a Beacon of Citizen Science: Regional Contributions, Macroecological Data Networks, and Strategies for Optimizing Taxonomic Identification Efficiency in India

programme.title: The Asian Nature Challenge as a Beacon of Citizen Science: Regional Contributions, Macroecological Data Networks, and Strategies for Optimizing Taxonomic Identification Efficiency in India
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract: The Asian Nature Challenge (ANC) represents a major milestone in decentralized biodiversity monitoring, serving as a powerful engine for global open-access macroecological data networks. By evaluating massive crowd-sourced datasets-specifically observations-740399.csv and observations-740433.csv-this cross-study analyzes the mechanics of regional participation, data quality, and taxonomic validation patterns across Asian nations. Empirically, the ANC acts as a beacon of citizen science, mobilizing tens of thousands of participants to generate over 190,000 observations, mapping critical target species, endemics, and geographic range extensions. However, comparative analysis reveals stark disparities in verification efficiency: while Taiwan and Japan achieve high Research Grade conversion rates of 62.97% and 56.08% respectively, India exhibits an identification bottleneck, converting only 40.11% of its 47,346 observations. Granular taxonomic breakdowns for India indicate high proficiency in ornithology (89.88%), contrasted against systemic deficits in mega-diverse groups such as Plantae (27.18%), Arachnida (30.89%), and Fungi (4.04%). These backlogs stem from a structural deficit in expert identifier networks relative to active field observers, alongside limitations in local computer vision models for complex tropical flora and micro-fauna. To scale up utility for formal scientific research, India must transition from raw data acquisition to active identification curation. Lessons from successful regional networks show this can be achieved by engineering dedicated expert-curator incentives, hosting targeted digital 'ID-a-thons', and integrating localized AI-assisted taxonomic vetting pipelines to streamline the validation flow.

actual.identification_notes: Second pre-recorded video by Ashwin A, introduced by the moderator; ASR renders the event as "Asia Nature Challenge". Co-authors named "Lavanya Patan and Prithvi Sharma" (ASR).

content_items.summary: Ashwin A analyses two years (2024-2025) of the Asian Nature Challenge on iNaturalist, about 190,000 observations, asking how efficiently observations become research-ready. India contributed about 47,000 observations but only about 40% reached research grade, compared with 60-79% for other countries, revealing an identification deficit that is taxonomically graded: birds and mammals reach research grade easily while plants and fungi are around 4%, a 22-fold spread. He proposes an identification flywheel: target backlogs, build identifier networks, run targeted mobilisation such as identification-a-thons and use AI-assisted, human-verified identification.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: More observations do not mean more usable data; identification capacity is the bottleneck for India's citizen science.
content_items.why_it_matters: It pinpoints where citizen-science pipelines stall and suggests targeted interventions to turn volume into research-ready records.

content_items.title: Growing Together: Community-Driven Conservation of Plant Genetic Resources

programme.title: Growing Together: Community-Driven Conservation of Plant Genetic Resources
programme.session: LT16: Community-Powered, Research-Ready: Citizen Science for a Digital Future
programme.abstract:
The EU project INCREASE (Intelligent Collections of Food Legumes Genetic Resources for European Agrofood Systems) fosters agricultural biodiversity through participatory research. With 28 partners from 14 countries, it focuses on legumes (chickpea, bean, lentil, lupin). A central component is the Citizen Science Experiment (CSE) with common bean across Europe. CSE aims to: increase citizen awareness, generate phenotypic data of 1130 bean lines across European environments, and test decentralized conservation approaches for germplasm conservation and multiplication.

Beans are distributed with the help of the INCREASE CSA mobile app, integrating observation and teaching tools, and legal frameworks (SMTA via FAO Easy SMTA interface). The system employs digital infrastructure for seed exchange with DOI registration via the FAO Global Information System GLIS, ensuring machine-actionable data provenance. Each citizen receives a bag with 5 PGR lines plus one commercial check variety. Citizens are assigned to Randomization Units based on latitude, elevation, and 3 bioclimatic variables to ensure environmental diversity.

Dissemination prioritizes native languages through voluntary translators, with partners recruiting in their own countries using all available media. Engagement is fostered via picture galleries, questionnaires, contests, and private Facebook groups. We share experiences designing a program balancing human-centric citizen science with modern biodiversity informatics requirements. The CSE attracted over 26,000 participants, including 650+ schools, fostering public education on PGR topics from an early age. We discuss how the INCREASE CSA app bridges community observations and research assets, demonstrating a scalable decentralized conservation model.

actual.identification_notes: Moderator introduces Markus Oppermann from Germany; matches programme.

content_items.summary: Markus Oppermann presents the citizen science experiment of the INCREASE project, which sent well-defined sets of common bean varieties to citizens across Europe via a smartphone app with a material agreement. Participants grew the beans, recorded defined traits and images, and could exchange material (with DOIs assigned), producing more than 100,000 phenotypic observations from about 25,000 registered participants in nearly every EU country since 2021. National Facebook groups, native-language support and country-specific media worked best, and the project had to cap shipments at 5,000 in the third round due to demand; it also tested decentralized, community-based conservation as an alternative to gene banks.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Giving citizens seeds, a good app and clear tutorials can yield large phenotypic datasets and community-based conservation of crop diversity.
content_items.why_it_matters: It demonstrates a scalable citizen-science model for plant genetic resources that both raises awareness and generates research data.
